answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1908–1970 · American psychologist, founder of humanistic psychology
answer.sourceLine: The vocabulary is genuinely his — “impulse-voices” is Maslow’s own coinage and runs through The Farther Reaches of Human Nature — but no book he published in his lifetime turns up in full-text search carrying this sentence. The earliest printing we could locate is Abraham H. Maslow: A Memorial Volume (Brooks/Cole, 1972) ↗, published two years after his death, where the line sits in what reads like a page of working notes.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually turns up

docMeta.dd: Abraham H. Maslow: A Memorial Volume

Runs directly into “Some more phrases to use:” — a list of formulations, not finished prose

source.excerpt: The way to recover the meaning of life and the worthwhileness of life is to recover the power of experience, to have impulse voices from within, and to be able to hear these impulse voices from within — and make the point: This can be done.
trail: Quote Investigator’s Abraham Maslow index ↗ carries no article on this line — the only Maslow saying it has investigated is the hammer-and-nail one — so there is no specialist finding to defer to here.

Wikiquote ↗ places the quote in its Attributed section and gives one citation: Richard T. Kinnier (ed.), The Meaning of Life: According to the Great and the Good (2007) — a modern anthology, not a Maslow source.

Full-text search across scanned books puts the sentence in a handful of volumes; the earliest is the 1972 memorial volume ↗. The same search shows Maslow’s own, different passage in The Farther Reaches of Human Nature about “experiential emptiness” and hearing “small, delicate impulse voices from within.”

The term itself is authentically his: Google Books reports eight pages of The Farther Reaches of Human Nature matching “impulse-voices” ↗, while “worthwhileness” and “power of experience” return nothing in that book.
source.excerptNote: That is the full sentence as printed. In the 1972 memorial volume the very next words are “Some more phrases to use:” — which is why we read this as a working note rather than a published statement.

source.rightsHolder: The estate of Abraham H. Maslow; Brooks/Cole Publishing Company (1972 memorial volume)
source.rightsNote: Everything Maslow wrote was published in 1931 or later — he was born in 1908 and died in 1970 — so no wording of his can be public domain in the United States on age alone. This particular sentence is first found in print in a 1972 posthumous volume, which places it firmly in copyright; short quotation with attribution, as here, is the normal basis for reproducing it.

author.name: Abraham Maslow
author.heading: Who Maslow actually was
author.bio: Abraham Maslow was the American psychologist who put the hierarchy of needs and the peak experience into everyday language, and who spent his later years at Brandeis arguing that psychology had studied damage far more carefully than it had studied flourishing. His central books — Motivation and Personality (1954), Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) and the posthumous The Farther Reaches of Human Nature (1971) — built the case that healthy people can be told apart from merely un-sick ones. He died of a heart attack in June 1970, leaving a large mass of notes, journals and lecture drafts that colleagues and his widow published afterwards.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong when this one travels
misattribution.intro: Nobody credits this to the wrong person — the trouble is that it is quoted as a finished Maslow aphorism when the documented text is a fragment of working notes, and the parts that give that away are the parts most often cut.

items.why: The circulating version usually stops at “hear these impulse voices from within.” In print the sentence continues “— and make the point: This can be done,” and in the 1972 memorial volume it is followed immediately by “Some more phrases to use:” ↗ — a writer’s note to himself, not a closing flourish.
Prints the middle clause out entirely: “…worthwhileness of life is to recover the power of experience. This can be done.” ↗ The impulse voices — the actual Maslow idea in the sentence — disappear.

items.who: Richard D. Zakia, Perceptual Quotes for Photographers
items.why: Renders it as “recover the power to experience” ↗ rather than “the power of experience” — a small change that shifts it from a faculty to be regained to an act to be performed.

items.who: Quote sites that name a Maslow book
items.why: Some pages pin the line to The Farther Reaches of Human Nature. Google Books returns no match for “worthwhileness” anywhere in that book ↗. Wikiquote, correspondingly, files the quote under “Attributed” ↗ and cites only a 2007 anthology.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are almost certainly Maslow’s, and the term “impulse-voices” is demonstrably his — but the sentence first surfaces in print in Abraham H. Maslow: A Memorial Volume (Brooks/Cole, 1972) ↗, after his death, as a note he was still working on.

context.heading: Why this one reads like an aphorism when it isn’t
lead: Maslow’s late work turns on a single worry: that modern people had gone quiet inside. In The Farther Reaches of Human Nature he calls the condition “experiential emptiness” — the absence of impulse voices from within — and describes therapy and education as ways of learning to hear those small, delicate impulse voices again ↗. That is the published, finished version of the thought.

The sentence people quote is the unfinished version. In the 1972 memorial volume it runs straight into the words “Some more phrases to use:” ↗ — the giveaway that what survives here is a writer stocking a list of formulations, with the instruction “make the point: This can be done” addressed to himself. Strip that tail off, as almost every quote site does, and a working note starts to read like a closing line.
detailsBody: The tell is in the punctuation. Genuine Maslow prose does not usually break mid-sentence into an imperative aimed at the author; outline notes do it constantly.

This is why the honest label here is “attributed” rather than “verified.” Nothing suggests someone else wrote it, and everything about the phrasing points to Maslow — but a line first printed after a writer’s death, in a memorial compilation, without a stated origin, is not the same evidentiary object as a page in a book he signed off on.
context.pull: “Make the point: This can be done” is not a claim. It is a reminder to himself to make one.
